author: nstarman
body:
Clicking a contents link on the CV scrolled to the right place and then highlighted the wrong section. Reported for **Select Publications**, which said *Professional Appointments*, and again for **Select Fellowships & Awards**, which said *Select Publications*.

Two causes, one behind the other.

## 1. The mark was never recomputed after a jump

This is the one that produced the reported behaviour, and the larger half.

The rail listened for `scroll` and `resize`. A fragment jump moves the viewport but cannot be relied on to deliver a `scroll` event for it, so clicking a contents link moved the page and **left the mark exactly where it was** — on whichever section the reader had been standing in before they clicked. That matches both screenshots: the mark is not "off by one", it is stale.

Three signals now, each covering a gap in the others:

- `hashchange` — a click on the rail, or any in-page anchor
- `scrollend` — a smooth scroll come to rest, guarded because it is not everywhere yet
- a click on the rail itself — for when the hash does not change, because the reader clicked the section they were already in

## 2. The landing position failed its own test

Underneath that, the comparison was also wrong, and would have shown up as a genuine off-by-one once the mark was being recomputed at all.

An anchor jump lands a heading exactly on its own `scroll-margin-top`, so in principle `top === topGap`. In practice the browser settles the scroll on a device pixel and the heading comes to rest a fraction **below** the line. Measured on the page:

```
positions          +0.24px      publications       +0.19px
awards-major       +0.06px      grants-major       +0.13px
software           +0.07px      talks-contributed  +0.20px
```

`top - topGap <= 0` therefore concluded the heading had not been reached and picked its predecessor. A one-pixel tolerance settles it — far more than the rounding, far less than the hundreds of pixels between consecutive headings, so it cannot reach forward to a section that is genuinely below.

That comparison moves out of the page's inline script into `src/lib/scrollspy.js` and takes numbers instead of elements, so the arithmetic is testable without a DOM.

## Verification

Six unit tests covering the comparison, including every landing delta measured off the page. Two fail against the old `<= 0` — checked by reverting the constant and watching them go red.

The behavioural half cannot be unit-tested without a DOM, so it was checked in a browser **against the built site**, not the dev server:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| contents links marking the wrong section | 14 of 15 | **0 of 15** |

Plus the two reported cases specifically (click Fellowships & Awards, click Publications), a click followed by further manual scrolling, and plain scrolling at five positions from the top of the page to the bottom — each checked against an independently computed expectation.

`npm test` — 173 unit tests, schema, BibTeX, build, a11y and links all pass.

## A note on how the first attempt got this wrong

The first commit claimed all fifteen links were fixed. That verification was invalid twice over, and both are worth recording because they are easy to repeat:

- The check dispatched a synthetic `scroll` event before reading the mark. That is precisely the signal the page was missing, so the test supplied the bug's own cure and then reported success.
- Later measurements ran against a dev server that was serving stale HTML — its HMR socket had dropped, and the page under test did not contain the edits at all. `curl | grep` on the served markup showed the new handler absent from the dev server and present in the build.

Everything above was re-measured against `npm run build` output after that was found.

author: masterplanner25
body:
Prompted by a plain question — *are we sure what our packages actually are?* Every first-party name was probed against PyPI rather than read out of a doc. Four things this repo asserted were wrong.

## 1. `CLAUDE.md` named the wrong directory for the A2A wire adapter

It called `C:\codev\nodus-a2a-wire` "the local worktree" of the wire repo. It is not:

| Directory | Remote | Branch | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `C:\dev\nodus-a2a` | `nodus-a2a` | `main`, clean | the published coordinator, 23 tests |
| `C:\codev\nodus-a2a-wire` | **`nodus-a2a`** | **detached at `10746ce`** | a worktree of the *coordinator* repo's old history |
| `C:\codev\a2a-wire-pub` | **`nodus-a2a-wire`** | `main` | the one that actually corresponds to the wire repo |

The directory named after the wire repo is the one that is not it, and following the old text would push wire-adapter commits at the coordinator.

Both `C:\codev` directories are **CrewAI-showcase artifacts** — nothing recorded that, and reading them as maintained companion checkouts is what made #477 look like a live defect.

## 2. The wire adapter is 188 tests, not 180

## 3. The companion count was stale by two

*"32 live on PyPI (33 counting nodus-lang)"* against a verified **34 + nodus-lang = 35** — and it was already wrong before `nodus-flow` was published. Replaced with a dated figure plus the method to re-derive it, because a hand-maintained count is the same failure mode as the version strings that section already refuses to carry. It also names the three first-party artifacts that deliberately are *not* on PyPI (`nodus-vscode`, `nodus-run-action`, `nodus-a2a-wire`), so the number cannot be "corrected" by counting them in.

## 4. `docs/ecosystem/README.md` hardcoded versions the manifest owns

Two consumer rows carried versions that `tools/consumers.json` is supposed to be authoritative for, and `nodus-mcp-server` was a patch behind. The consumer rows point at the manifest now. **The other seven hardcoded versions in that table were each checked against PyPI and are accurate**, so the table was not restructured.

## Plus: `nodus-flow` is now tracked by `check_publish_drift`

It never was, under either name — so a published first-party package sat outside the sweep that asks whether a companion has drifted from what it published. 10/10 match.

## Verified, not inferred

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `check_downstream_constraints` | 6/6 companions admit 5.5.0 |
| `check_publish_drift` | 10/10 match what they published |
| PyPI probe | 35 projects live; 3 first-party names deliberately absent |
| `--static` / `--runtime` / `--versions` / `--closed-issues` | 135/135 · 251/251 · 15/15 · 1/1 |
| `ruff` | clean |

## #477 re-scoped on the issue, not here

From *"the A2A wire protocol is uninstallable"* to what it is: **an unfinished showcase spin-off**. Nothing depends on it, no install path advertises it, and the GitHub repo already exists — so the "give it its own repo" half of its recommendation is already done. Relabelled `severity:low`.

Its blocking detail is worse than filed, though: the repo's `main` still carries `nodus-lang>=4.0.0,<5.0.0` (added in `51292f3`), so even after a rename, publishing would produce something uninstallable alongside any 5.x — the `ResolutionImpossible` of #445.

body:
## Summary

Centre the project name in a route's floating bar and make it the control that returns a reader to the top of the route they are reading.

## Key Changes

- Lay `[data-bar-row]` in `route-bar.astro` as three columns with equal outer ones, so the name centres against the row whatever the two controls beside it weigh.
- Render the name as a `<button>` carrying `aria-label="Back to top of <route>"`, the 44px minimum, and the underline treatment its sibling lockup uses.
- Scroll to the top on activation and clear any fragment a rail row left behind, reusing the pattern `site-bar.astro` already applies to its own home control.
- Toggle `inert` alongside the existing shown marker, so the control leaves the pointer and the tab sequence together while it is unpainted.
- Add four guards to `e2e/case-studies.spec.ts` covering the centring per route, the accessible name, the back-to-top with its fragment clearing, and the withheld tab stop.
- Record the decision in `.claude/ARCHITECTURE.md`, scope the exit count in `.claude/REQUIREMENTS.md`, and update `.claude/wireframes/site-bar.md` and `.claude/context/case-study-navigation.md`.

## Technical Context

- Three items under `justify-between` split the free space into two equal gaps, which centres the middle one only when the two flanking it match. The lockup measures 79px against the toggle's 44px, so the name sat `(79 - 44) / 2` right of centre at every width and on all five routes. Equal outer columns state the relationship the centring depends on, where a 17.5px offset would encode today's two control widths.
- A guard reading the gap between the two flanking controls passes against that defect, since equal gaps are exactly what the previous layout produced. It reads the row's own box instead.
- The name is a control because a route had no way back to its own top. The lockup here and the closing foot both target the landing page, and the rail's first row is the only control that returns to the top and is hidden below 1280. `.claude/REQUIREMENTS.md` § Navigation now scopes its two-control count to exits, so an in-route control does not read as a third one.

## Testing

- [x] `bun run check` passes: lint, format, spell, typecheck, 23 unit tests, build.
- [x] `bun run test:e2e` passes across chromium, firefox, and webkit: 812 passed, 7 skipped, 0 failed.
- [x] Name centres to 0.00px from the row's centre at 320, 390, 640, 768, 1024, 1280, 1440, and 1920, on all five routes.
- [x] Widest label at 390 measures 96x44, clearing the phone tap minimum on both axes.
- [x] Each new guard run against the defect it catches: reverting the grid fails the five centring guards alone, disabling the click fails the back-to-top alone, and dropping `inert` fails the reachability guard alone.
- [x] Activation by pointer and by Enter both land at scroll 0 and clear a `#fragment`.
- [x] Touch behaviour on a phone or tablet (operator, needs the device; emulation reproduces the events and not the pointer hardware).

## Live smoke

Read against the dev server at `localhost:4325` on all five routes. The operator confirmed the centring and the back-to-top on the running page before this branch was committed.

Measured on the built preview, `/diction` unless noted:

```plaintext
width | homeW  tglW | offset from bar centre | label box | collide | sideways
  320 |  79.0  44.0 |                +0.00px |     78x44 | clear   | no
  390 |  79.0  44.0 |                +0.00px |     78x44 | clear   | no
  768 |  79.0  44.0 |                +0.00px |     78x44 | clear   | no
 1280 |  79.0  44.0 |                +0.00px |     78x44 | clear   | no
 1920 |  79.0  44.0 |                +0.00px |     78x44 | clear   | no

/jobtriage  offset=+0.00px  label= 96x44  clear  aria="Back to top of Jobtriage"
/aitk       offset=+0.00px  label= 57x44  clear  aria="Back to top of aitk"

at top of route:    inert=true  data-shown=null  opacity=0  focus reached=false
scrolled into prose: inert=false data-shown=true opacity=1  focus reached=true

before: scrollY=3000 hash="#problem"
after : scrollY=0    hash=""
```

## For the reviewer

- Confirm an in-route control reads as distinct from the two exits rather than as the third control `.claude/REQUIREMENTS.md` § Navigation rules out. The scoping line added there is the argument, and it is the one judgment in this branch that a measurement cannot settle.

author: erichowens
body:
## Summary

Erich asked why `pd-red-team` "never seems to work." Investigated rather than guess:

**It does work.** Verified on #9866: it fired ~2 hours after the PR opened and posted one real MEDIUM finding (a GitHub Actions permissions issue on a job running PR-head scripts with a write-scoped token), which I independently checked against the actual workflow file and confirmed was real — not fabricated — then fixed.

**Why it looks broken:** its own spec (`fleet/ships/red-team.md`) states silence *is* the success state — "posting 'no attacks landed' prose is the failure mode." Unlike every other review ship (qa, lookout, spark, spider, code-reviewer), which always posts something, red-team is designed to stay silent on a clean run. That's not a bug.

**But there's a real bug underneath it.** `decideShipGate`'s `SECURITY_SURFACE_RE` (`apps/fleet-executor/src/gates.ts`) decides whether red-team even spawns, tested against each changed file *path*, before any AI spend — and it only matched `crypto|sign|verify|hash|token|secret|auth|capabilit`. None of `core/kernel/pd-vault/src/hpke.rs`, `core/kernel/pd-vault/src/keys.rs`, `apps/relay/src/device-keys.ts`, or a `*-device-keys.sql` migration contain any of those substrings — so red-team silently never ran on either #9873 (the HPKE key-wrap crypto primitive) or #9882 (the device-key registry routes), the two most security-relevant PRs shipped this session. Every other ship fired normally on both; only red-team's own pre-filter was blind to them.

## Fix

Widen `SECURITY_SURFACE_RE` to also match `key|vault|wrap|hpke` — the minimal set directly evidenced by the two real diffs that fell through the gap. Per this same file's own stated philosophy for the analogous `UNREVIEWABLE_PATH_RE` gate ("a false negative here silently hides real code from review, which is far worse than the tokens a false positive costs"), erring toward running red-team more often is the correct direction to widen in.

## Test Plan

```
cd apps/fleet-executor && npx tsc --noEmit   → clean
cd apps/fleet-executor && npx vitest run     → Test Files 54 passed (54), Tests 920 passed (920)
node scripts/assemble-changelog.mjs --check  → ✓ 15 fragment(s) clean
```

New test in `gates.test.ts` asserts the gate now runs on the exact four real paths from #9873/#9882 that previously fell through.

## Roadmap link

Roadmap-Item: none — a targeted bug fix to the fleet review infrastructure, not a roadmap-tracked feature.

## Changelog & Parsimony

- [x] New `changelog.d/draft-red-team-gate-key-vault.md` fragment added
- [x] Minimal, single-line regex change plus a regression test — no unrelated scope

author: rynfar
body: ## Problem Prime Agent 0.8.1 can cancel its recursive descendant-quiescence wait when a parent deletes its final child after receiving the child reply. Pylon treated that internal cancellation as terminal, so the turn failed before the continued root response arrived. ## Fix Retry only the exact native quiescence-cancellation result, on the same daemon connection generation, with a three-retry bound. The retry reissues only the read-only completion barrier and never resends the prompt. The active turn abort signal suppresses retries for user cancellation, while disposal, reconnect ambiguity, unrelated failures, and repeated cancellation still fail closed. author: johnnyc9000
body:
Stacked on #249 — please merge that first. This depends on `combine-records.js`, which only exists on that branch.

**Scope: `leo-connector-common` only.** This PR adds the delete fan-out that `rstreams-connector-datalake` needs. It changes no connector implementation, so **Redshift behavior is unchanged**.

## Problem

A delete keyed by something other than the row's natural key — a parent FK like `shipment_id`, or a source `mongo_id` — is synthesized as a `_del_<value>` marker. `combine()` groups by natural key, so that marker lands in a group of its own and is never compared against the same-batch writes for the rows it affects.

The outcome is then decided by the connector's fixed flush-before-merge order rather than by event order. Net effect: **if any write for the row exists in the batch, the delete is reverted**, regardless of which event was actually later on the bus.

Confirmed live in production on `f_shipment_item`, `f_order_item_activity` and `f_warehouse`; structurally present on 18 tables.

## Approach

The ordering logic was never missing. `combineRecords` already implements last-event-wins correctly — the markers just never reached it. So resolve the delete to the natural keys it currently matches and emit one marker per row. Those flow through the existing logic unchanged.

- **`common/datawarehouse/delete-fanout.js`** (new) — the fan-out, extracted for testability, same reason `combine-records.js` was split out of `combine.js`.
- **`common/datawarehouse/load.js`** — `checkforDelete` delegates to it.

### Resolution is an optional client capability

`load.js` is shared by every connector — postgres, mysql, oracle, sqlserver, mongo, elasticsearch. Raw SQL there would break or misbehave for all of them, so the fan-out asks the client for an optional `resolveDeleteKeys(table, field, nk, ids, cb)`.

A connector that does not implement it — plus any table with a composite natural key, or one absent from `tableConfig` — **falls back to today's `_del_` marker**. That is every connector in this repo, including postgres, so nothing here changes behavior for existing consumers.

The Databricks connector implements the capability in its own repo ([rstreams-connector-datalake `fix/rpl-6780-resolve-delete-keys`](https://github.com/Chub-Engineering/rstreams-connector-datalake/tree/fix/rpl-6780-resolve-delete-keys)), so only that path changes.

### Also fixes a latent case

When a table's natural key is not named `id` (`f_shipping_label_package`, NK `package_id`), the old marker left the natural key unset. Every such delete hashed to the same empty combine key and all but the last were silently dropped — data loss, not just misordering. No producer targets that table today, so this was latent.

## Tests

16 new, all passing. Includes RPL-6780's five ordering scenarios replayed through a resolved marker; rows 1 and 4 — the two the ticket calls provably wrong today — now come out correct. Also covers every fallback path, resolver errors, and the non-`id` natural key case.

Suite is 23 passing / 1 failing. **That failure (`test/checksum/index.test.js`) is pre-existing on this branch's base** — not introduced here. Lint error counts are identical to base on both files touched.

## Not in this PR

- **Any connector implementation.** The Databricks `resolveDeleteKeys` lives in its own repo and PR. Until it lands and the datalake pin moves off `4.1.0-rc.32056762820`, nothing in production changes.
- **Residual gap.** A row created in the *same* batch as the delete does not exist when the target is queried, so it is not resolved. Not a regression — the previous FK-keyed UPDATE also ran before the merge and matched nothing. Closing it needs the reconciliation sweep described on RPL-6780.
- **End-to-end verification.** RPL-6780 asks for positive exercise across all 18 tables in non-prod. These are unit tests; they prove the fan-out logic, not end-to-end behavior. That gate is still open.

## Note on the commit list

The branch history includes DPT-2586 numeric-validation commits and a postgres `resolveDeleteKeys` implementation, both since reverted in full — DPT-2586 is being issued separately, and the postgres work was dropped to keep this branch focused on the fan-out. `common/utils/validation.js` and `postgres/lib/dwconnect.js` are byte-identical to the base branch. The net diff is three files. History was preserved rather than rewritten because the branch was already pushed.

> **Medium Risk**
> Changes the shared DW load delete path used by every connector; behavior stays on the old path until a client implements `resolveDeleteKeys`, but async fan-out and new failure modes affect all delete events once connectors opt in.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes **RPL-6780**, where deletes keyed by a parent FK or other non–natural-key column were emitted as `_del_<value>` markers that **never joined the same `combine()` group** as that row’s writes, so batch flush order could **silently undo a delete** even when the delete was later on the bus.
> 
> **`load.js`** now routes `type: 'delete'` events through a new **`delete-fanout.js`** module instead of inlining marker synthesis. The fan-out emits **one delete marker per affected row**. When the delete field is already the table’s single-column natural key, behavior is unchanged. Otherwise it optionally calls **`client.resolveDeleteKeys(table, field, nk, ids, cb)`** to look up current natural keys and build markers keyed by the real NK (so **`combineRecords` last-event-wins** applies). Connectors without that hook, composite NKs, or unknown tables **still get the historical `_del_` marker**. Resolver errors propagate instead of dropping the delete. The same change also fixes a latent bug for NKs not named `id` (e.g. `package_id`), where markers previously collapsed to one combine group.

author: thek3nsai
body:
One entry, beside the existing `gh pr merge --delete-branch` gotcha — a different hazard of the same command.

## What happened

Merging #97 with `--delete-branch` left the checkout on a local `main` that was 5 ahead / 3 behind origin. Two of the five commits were the pre-squash form of #96 and already on `main` inside the squash; three were rulings that had never been pushed in any form. `git reset --hard origin/main` would have destroyed them silently.

The trap is that **squashing rewrites SHAs**, so every pre-squash commit reports "not on any remote branch" forever — `git branch -r --contains` said local-only for all five, which is true and useless. It cannot distinguish "already shipped under a different SHA" from "genuinely unpushed".

## What the entry records

- Compare **content, not SHAs**: `git diff --stat <local-branch> <squash-commit>` isolates the real divergence in one command, then confirm per-commit with a distinctive string.
- Tag before resetting; the reflog is not a plan.
- The second-order trap: this repo squash-merges, so local `main` drifts **by default**. Combined with launcher symlinks resolving through the checkout, a stale `main` silently runs old client code while the PR says the fix is merged — which is exactly the "healthy-looking state in front of a broken one" shape the *Live messaging* section already collects.

Content-only change; the three rescued rulings themselves landed in #98.

Final release-review change for `ai-sdlc-v2.4.0` after the consulting-playbook adapter was repinned, conformance-tagged, rebound in the control-plane registry, and PR #55 merged green.

The manual all-target release verification run `32994748740` exposed a circular release-gate defect: `consulting-playbook` correctly pins the future `ai-sdlc-v2.4.0` receiver, but the normal verifier required that not-yet-created control-plane tag to resolve before the documented pre-publication verification step could pass. This PR now resolves that contradiction without creating the tag early or weakening normal immutable verification.

## Publishable release state
- release: `ai-sdlc-v2.4.0`
- previous known good: `ai-sdlc-v2.3.2` @ `5738ace3ee90dde11336f8f8099e64e5645f7139`

## Boundary
This PR does not itself create the `ai-sdlc-v2.4.0` tag, run REAL acceptance, invoke Codex, create an implementation branch/PR, merge generated work, release generated work, or deploy anything. author: glennjacobs
body:
Companion to #2653. Same automation, ported to `2.x`.

## Why this PR is necessary, not just tidy

`pull_request_target` reads the workflow **and its config** from the PR's base branch. A PR targeting `2.x` runs `2.x`'s copy. Without this PR, 2.x PRs get no triage, no review and no version label at all.

The reverse is also worth knowing: `issues` and `schedule` events only ever fire from the **default branch**, so `issue-triage.yml`, `issue-digest.yml`, `issue-stale.yml` and the issue form are inert here today. They're included anyway so the automation survives the default-branch flip at v2 GA without anyone having to remember.

## The interesting part: 2.x needed real changes, not a copy

The first four commits cherry-pick clean. The last one exists because **the review skill was written for 1.x and is actively wrong here** — not merely stale. Left alone it would have raised `Blocker`-severity findings against correct, idiomatic 2.x code on most core PRs, which is exactly how a review bot loses trust in its first week.

What differs:

| | `1.x` | `2.x` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Root namespace | `Lunar\` | `Lunar\Core\`, `Lunar\Panel\`, `Lunar\Filament\` |
| Model contracts | interface per model in `Models/Contracts/` | **none** |
| Type hints | concrete model is a Blocker | concrete model is **correct** |
| Filament `$model` | must be `FooContract::class` | correctly `Foo::class` |
| `Contracts/` | one interface per model | service contracts (`CartSession`, `ModelManifest`) |
| Migration base | `Lunar\Base\Migration` | `Lunar\Core\Database\Migration` |
| Money | `Lunar\DataTypes\Price` | `Lunar\Core\DataObjects\PriceValue` |
| Model traits | `Lunar\Base\Traits\` | `Lunar\Core\Models\Concerns\` |

Verified against the tree, not assumed — e.g. `packages/core/src/Pipelines/Cart/CalculateLines.php` type-hints `Lunar\Core\Models\Cart` directly, and `BrandResource` sets `$model = Brand::class`.

The model-contract category is replaced with a note saying it doesn't apply, plus the check that *does*: models are still swappable via `Lunar\Core\Manifests\ModelManifest`, which discovers classes extending `Lunar\Core\Models\Base` — so a new model that doesn't extend `Base` is a genuine finding.

The "Public API surface" section is reframed for pre-GA: breaking changes are allowed when deliberate, but need a matching Rector rule in `packages/upgrade` or consumers coming from 1.x are stranded.

**This also fixes the interactive `/lunar:pr-review` skill on this branch**, which had the same problem.

## Shared config, one file

`.claude/triage-rules.md` describes both layouts in one file rather than forking per branch — a path that doesn't exist on the branch being triaged simply never matches. That's why the first four commits cherry-picked without conflict.

## Noticed but not fixed

`fix-code-style.yml` on this branch runs `pint --diff=origin/1.x`, so on `2.x` it diffs against the wrong line. Out of scope here — flagging it rather than bundling an unrelated fix.

## Before this does anything

Same prerequisites as #2653: create the labels, add `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, set the Console cap. Merge #2653 first.

author: oshanyelena
body:
## Summary

Two more bugs found while dry-running the courtroom negotiation end-to-end against the real OpenAI API (`gpt-4o-mini`), independent of the turn-sequencing fix in #1.

### 1. Responder argued the wrong term, grounded in the wrong ontology entry

`pipeline.py`'s `_role_trigger()` already normalises the trigger passed to `ProposalGenerator` so that `trigger.source_term` always means *"this role's own term"*, regardless of who's speaking. But both `proposal_generator.py`'s `_term_for_role()` and `llm_reasoner.py`'s `generate()` re-applied the same initiator/responder branching on top of that already-normalised trigger, undoing the swap. The responder ended up being told to argue the *initiator's* term and grounding its evidence against the wrong ontology entry entirely.

Verified live: before the fix, the responder's prompt read `Term (yours): price` (the initiator's term, wrong). After the fix, it correctly reads `Term (yours): rate`, grounded against the real counterpart ontology definition (`"A recurring financial charge applied per billing period... Distinct from a one-time offer price."`).

Fix: removed the redundant role-branching in both call sites — `ProposalGenerator.generate()` is only ever called from `pipeline.negotiate()`, which always passes the already role-adjusted trigger.

### 2. Debate outcome never affected the final mapping confidence

`agreed_mapping.confidence` was always set to `trigger.confidence` — the original, static, detection-time similarity score — and was never updated by anything that happened during the negotiation. This meant a genuinely low-confidence trigger (e.g. 0.3) could **never** clear `HeuristicEvaluator`'s `CONTENT_LOW=0.40` override floor, no matter how strong the courtroom argumentation turned out to be. That defeats the entire purpose of the `evidence_heavy_debate` strategy, whose whole job is to resolve low-confidence/unknown-term situations through debate.

Fix: `pipeline.resolve()` now blends the trigger's starting confidence with the dialogue's own heuristic score: `(trigger.confidence + dialogue_score) / 2`. A strong debate can now rescue a low starting point, and a weak one still drags a mapping down.

Verified live: starting confidence 0.3 + dialogue score 0.7875 → blended confidence 0.5438 → decision flipped from a forced `reject` to `accept`, and the mapping persisted correctly to the SQLite store (`price ↔ rate, closeMatch, 0.5437`).

## Verification

- Ran the full negotiation pipeline against the **real OpenAI API** (not mocked) with two genuinely different ontologies — the existing `hotel_v1.owl` fixture (`price`) and a new, deliberately conflicting finance definition of `rate` — to confirm the responder now grounds in the correct, different definition and real disagreement is possible.
- Confirmed via live trace inspection that the blended confidence is used consistently for both the provisional and final `agreed_mapping`, and that an `accept` decision now correctly persists to `MappingStore`.
- Full existing test suite: **211/211 passed**, unchanged, both before and after (this fix has zero prior test coverage of the responder-role path, which is exactly why it went undetected).

## Notes for reviewers

author: dgmlnr
body:
## El último pendiente

El alto desaprovechado en teléfonos. La causa era un `min()` que ponía el tamaño **por tramo** como techo:

| ventana | altura permitía | el tramo daba | sobraba |
|---|---|---|---|
| 390×844 | 119px | **60px** | 363px de pantalla vacía |
| 1440×900 | 119px | 170px (no bindeaba) | 0 — ya funcionaba |

**La carta en un teléfono pasa de 60 a 106px.** Nada cambia en desktop, y nada cambia **inline** — esa regla no aplica ahí: un widget embebido en el artículo de otro no es dueño del viewport.

## Lo que el techo venía tapando

**1. Ninguna ventana vertical.** Las cinco de `table-viewport-fit` eran más anchas que altas — o sea, *una sola forma*. Y justo la altura es el eje escaso en la otra. Mientras el tramo acotaba desde arriba, un residual mal declarado no se podía notar. Apenas la ventana empezó a decidir: **41px de desborde en 1v1**, más en 2v2.

**2. El residual estaba medido sólo en apaisado.** Los teléfonos angostos tienen el suyo ahora, acotado por ancho de shell — que es lo que el shell puede consultar, y cae donde corresponde: un teléfono apaisado mide 844 de ancho y conserva los valores de siempre.

**3. El mazo se fue del paño.** Es una fracción de una **carta**, así que creció con ellas: 10px afuera, cortado. Anclado al borde de la mano en vez de eso, aterrizó **encima de la tercera carta** — porque a ese ancho quedan cinco píxeles entre la mano y el carril de la manija. Ninguna forma de anclar inventa lugar que no está. Va despejado de la fila.

## Dos cercados que pasaban sobre el bug

- El del mazo medía **un** ancho, el del arnés, donde la mano es angosta y sobra lugar al costado.
- El de "el mazo entra en el paño" **repartía con otro asiento**, no con el del espectador — que es de donde vino el reporte.

Los dos recorren ahora anchos de teléfono y el asiento propio, y fallan con los números exactos.

## Verificación

1769 tests, `tsc -b` y eslint limpios, visuales 20/20.

author: fx
body:
## Summary

Documentation only. Running the merged server against real Sonarr, Radarr, and Prowlarr instances surfaced four issues; three of them the specs did not cover well enough to call the implementation wrong. This amends the specs where they were silent or self-contradictory, and adds a change document for each finding plus one for npm publishing.

No source, test, config, or workflow file is touched. Everything described here is planned work.

## Spec amendments

**Architecture** gains a Packaging and Release section: public npm distribution, build output only, documentation that presents the published package as the default path, versions derived from commit history rather than hand-edited, no release from a commit whose gates have not passed, an explicit human action before publishing, and no long-lived registry credential in the repository.

**Tool Contracts** gains three amendments, one per finding. A published input schema must describe every argument the tool accepts, and variants must be published as declared alternatives of an object schema — the previous wording required both a closed published schema and root-level discriminated unions, which the protocol cannot express at once, so an implementation could satisfy one requirement only by breaking the other. An error summary must carry its stable code and remediation hint, because a caller may see only the summary when a call reports failure. A capability result must be bounded by default.

**Library Management** gains calendar anchoring: an entry anchors to the date that placed it inside the requested window and names which date that was. The spec had never said which of a Radarr movie's three release dates anchors it, so the current fixed precedence was not wrong by the letter.

## Change documents

| # | Change | Covers |
|---|--------|--------|
| 0011 | npm Publishing | release-please, MIT license, OIDC trusted publishing with provenance, and README rewritten around `npx mcp-arr` |
| 0012 | Published Tool Schemas | thirteen of fifteen tools publish an empty input schema |
| 0013 | Result Summary Fidelity | error summaries drop code and remediation; capability report is unbounded |
| 0014 | Calendar Anchoring | Radarr entries anchored outside the requested window |

## What the live testing found

Thirteen of fifteen tools publish `{"type":"object","properties":{}}` over `tools/list`. Validation is unaffected — it runs against the full typed union, so every call is checked exactly as intended — which is why this survived: the server behaves correctly on every call it receives and simply never tells a caller what to send. A host that filters arguments against the published schema cannot call the domain surface at all.

Radarr calendar entries are anchored by a fixed digital, physical, cinema precedence that ignores the query window. Querying August 2026 returned six movies, four of which reported an anchor outside that window — one by nearly four years.

Error summaries discard the code and remediation the structured result carries: an unsupported variant summarizes as `sonarr error, radarr error` while the structured result holds `unsupported_capability` and an actionable hint. Separately, `arr_capabilities` enumerates every unimplemented operation for every application, roughly eight thousand tokens against three live instances, on the one call an agent makes to orient itself.

## Ordering

Changes 0011 through 0014 are scheduled ahead of the pending 0004 through 0010, recorded in prose in both indexes. Their `depends_on` fields are left empty and 0004 through 0010 were deliberately not edited to depend on them: ordering preference is not a dependency, and encoding it as one would have been dishonest modelling. 0012 is the one worth landing before any further domain change, since every one of them adds tools onto the same publication path.

## Note on the .gitignore hunk

One line, unrelated to the spec work, included deliberately: it ignores `.mcp.json`, which holds real instance URLs and API keys for local host configuration. Leaving the rule uncommitted would keep that protection local to one checkout.

## Review

Codex reviewed the branch with the full scope brief and found no blocking defects, independently confirming that the amended object-root published-schema requirement is satisfiable.

Two Open Questions in the change documents need answers before implementation: the GitHub App ID for release-please is absent from the repository (only the private key is set), and 0014 needs a decision on which date wins when several fall inside the same calendar window.

author: ha-dong-hai
body:
# [MLACP-100] Hoàn tiền được xử lý qua VNPay sandbox

Jira: MLACP-100 · CF3-S2-BE11

## Description
Ported the reference ledger-reversal logic (D8 proportional reversal, settlement
tranche shrinking, Payment.Refunded flip) — but the reference implementation itself
never actually calls VNPay, so the task's core DONE WHEN ("refund processed via
VNPay sandbox") had no code to port. Researched VNPay's official Merchant API refund
spec and implemented it from scratch.

## Changes
- `IVnPayService.RefundAsync` — new third signing scheme distinct from the existing
  two (CreatePaymentUrl / VerifyCallback): raw field values joined by `|` in VNPay's
  documented order, HMACSHA512, no URL-encoding, POSTed as JSON to VNPay's Merchant
  API transaction endpoint (`/merchant_webapi/api/transaction`, vnp_Command=refund) —
  a different endpoint and payload shape from the two payment-redirect flows.
- `VnPaySettings.RefundApiUrl` (defaults to the official sandbox endpoint).
- `ProcessRefundRequestCommandHandler` now calls VNPay first; ledger is only written
  and the refund only marked Approved if VNPay confirms `vnp_ResponseCode=00`.
  Failure throws `ExternalServiceException` (503), leaving the refund request
  untouched at Pending rather than recording a refund that didn't happen.
- `ProcessRefundRequestCommand` gained `ClientIpAddress` (VNPay requires the calling
  server's IP in the signed payload).
- Registered a named `"vnpay"` HttpClient in DI alongside the existing named clients.

## Change details
Two commits on `MLACP-100-hoan-tien-qua-vnpay`:
- `5988141` — ledger-only cut, gap disclosed (first pass, before research).
- `e2f6613` — adds the real VNPay call per the official spec.

## Impact range
`Application/Refunds/Commands/ProcessRefundRequest/*`, `IVnPayService.cs`,
`VnPayService.cs`, `VnPaySettings.cs`, `Api/Controllers/AdminController.cs`,
`Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs`, `appsettings.json`.

## Testing
`dotnet build MusicLounge.sln --configuration Release` — 0 warnings, 0 errors.
Not live-tested against VNPay sandbox: VNPay's own documentation states refund is
gated on the sandbox account and requires contacting VNPay support to enable it —
a business/support blocker independent of whether the code is correct.

## Operating requirements
Before this can be exercised end-to-end, someone needs to request refund access on
the VNPay sandbox merchant account (support ticket with VNPay), and `RefundApiUrl`
should be pointed at the production endpoint before go-live.

author: tristan-stoltz-erc
body:
## Summary

Compose the clock-provenance contract from #102 underneath the chemical-to-root handoff from #101, then fix the remaining timestamp semantic mismatch at the root boundary.

This is a non-destructive integration layer. The composition commit has two parents (#101 exact head and #102 exact head) and replaces only the `crates/domains/symthaea-chemosensation` subtree with the exact #102 subtree. The only new hand-written integration changes are in the bridge implementation and bridge README.

## Problem

Root `ModalInput::new(...)` assigns a Unix-epoch-relative **ingestion timestamp**. Chemical evidence may instead carry:

- an explicit Unix-epoch acquisition timestamp,
- a device-local/monotonic acquisition timestamp, or
- a numeric timestamp with no declared clock domain.

The previous bridge unconditionally did:

```rust
modal_input.timestamp = Duration::from_micros(projection.latest_timestamp_us);
```

That could turn a device uptime counter such as `123456 us` into a fake Unix timestamp near 1970.

## New timestamp contract

`ChemicalRootProjection` remains authoritative for source acquisition provenance:

```text
(clock_domain, earliest_timestamp_us, latest_timestamp_us)
```

Root `ModalInput.timestamp` now follows an asymmetric policy:

- explicit `ChemicalClockDomainId::unix_epoch()` -> preserve the source acquisition timestamp exactly;
- device-local declared clock -> keep source time on the projection and retain `ModalInput::new`'s root ingestion timestamp;
- unspecified source clock -> keep the numeric source time on the projection and retain root ingestion timestamp.

No source-clock field is added to public `ModalInput`, avoiding a source-breaking struct change.

## Clock-aware chemical contract composed from #102

The exact #102 chemosensation subtree supplies:

- canonical bounded `ChemicalClockDomainId`
- no implicit epoch (`None` never means Unix)
- backward wire migration of legacy observations to explicit clock-unspecified evidence
- v2 raw observation/evidence identities that include clock provenance
- shared-clock gating before multi-source skew calculations
- clock-aware temporal cognition with abstention rather than chemical rejection when the clock is absent
- shared-clock gating before olfactory/gustatory flavor temporal binding
- source clock retention in novelty traceability and root projections
- independent projector revalidation of publicly constructible clock metadata
- simulator regressions proving deterministic nose/tongue fixtures do not invent acquisition clocks

## Important time-integrity boundary

Equal `ChemicalClockDomainId` values establish a **declared comparison domain**, not measured synchronization quality. The ID alone does not prove offset error, oscillator stability, continuity, authenticity, or a bound on timestamp uncertainty.

Symthaea already has adjacent timing concepts in mesh-time consensus and HAL time-integrity work (offset/RTT/stratum/drift/quality; clock-source identity, reboot epoch, monotonicity, discontinuity/rate checks). This PR deliberately does not duplicate those into a chemical-only confidence scalar.

Before physical multi-device olfactory/gustatory fusion is activated, acquisition should provide a generic time-integrity/synchronization receipt with an explicit uncertainty/error bound, ideally extracted into a reusable timing contract. Multi-source hardware validation must not treat clock-domain equality itself as synchronization proof.

## Bridge regressions

The bridge tests now require:

1. unclocked source evidence preserves its source timestamp in `ChemicalRootProjection` but uses root ingestion time in `ModalInput`;
2. device-local clock evidence preserves `(clock_domain, source timestamp)` on the projection but uses root ingestion time;
3. explicit Unix-epoch acquisition time is copied exactly to `ModalInput.timestamp`;
4. lineage, confidence, BinaryHV, stable modality IDs, and defined-but-unconfigured fusion behavior remain unchanged;
5. adding unconfigured olfactory evidence still cannot change legacy visual fusion.

## Scope / non-claims

No clock synchronization protocol, no synchronization accuracy bound, no hardware, no root topology activation, no chemesthetic alias, no trust/authenticity claim, and no subjective smell/taste claim.

Keep draft until #101, #102, and the dedicated Chemosensation/root gates execute successfully on this exact composed head. Do not merge this integration PR ahead of its prerequisites.

author: highfeed
body:
The hourly volume chart opened with its first bar cut to a third: 20 px of a 30 px bar fell outside the plot.

This is not the clipping #54 fixed. That was the *end of the data*, where a bar centred on the last sample had nowhere to put its outer half; `x.padding` gave it room. This is the *window*: `range: [0.62, 1]` opens 62% of the way through the extent, which lands part-way through a bar, and a bar the window edge crosses is drawn with only the part that fits.

Bars are centred on their samples, so opening on a sample centre would still cut that bar exactly in half — my first attempt at this used `0.674`, the centre of sample 48, and measured 17 px of 35 showing. The window has to open half a bar earlier. `0.669` is sample 48 less half a bar, once the padding from #54 is counted in the extent.

Measured on the live chart objects at 1140 px, counting only bars with pixels inside the plot:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| first visible bar | 20 px of 30 cut off | whole |
| last visible bar | whole | whole |
| samples shown | 27 | 24 |

The window is also a round 24 hours now, which is what the chart's heading claims.

### Note for the reviewer

`0.669` is tied to this series being 72 hourly samples with `padding: 0.006`. Change `h72` and the number needs recomputing — the comment above it says how it is derived. The alternative is eight lines of arithmetic in the demo to derive it at runtime, which seemed worse for a page whose job is to be read.

The price chart drives this window and the volume chart follows it over `rangechange`; both extents stay identical and the shared window resolves to the same instant on both (0 s drift).

`node scripts/check-examples.mjs` passes, `npm test` is green.

author: manuerumx
body:
Completes **M4** for Django: the L2 query path, the three items #73 deferred, and the cross-language test the project exists to make runnable. Three commits, 33 files, +2861/−74.

**No cryptographic surface changes.** No envelope byte, derived value, vector expectation, error code, registry entry, or `pinned_decisions` key. Both conformance reports stay **144/144** with identical six-key sets. **No backfill** — the index column has been written correctly since #73.

Adapter **68 → 159** tests · Python core **294 → 304** · TypeScript **287 → 295**.

---

## 1. L2: the rewrite was the easy half

`filter(email=...)` and `__in` compile onto the blind-index sibling as `Lookup` subclasses, so they compose with `Q`, joins and subqueries for free. `docs/12` §3.2's deferred decision is settled as **option C**: `FieldsealQuerySet._fetch_all` re-verifies by default, `.candidates()` opts out. The rejected alternative — an explicit `.verified()` — fails *silently*: one forgotten call returns collision rows, which is the §10.2 wrong answer the adapter exists to prevent.

**The manager installs itself**, because a default you must install by hand is not a default. `class_prepared` attaches `FieldsealManager` to models declaring none of their own — Django flags its auto-created `objects` with `auto_created`, an exact test for "the author did not choose". Where they *did* choose, the adapter does not overwrite it; new check **E008** asks them to mix the queryset in.

### The design work: what shrinks

Verification drops rows **after** the database has applied `COUNT`, `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, so every method answered from SQL is wrong by default. Each bypass was checked against Django 6.1's source, not assumed:

| Surface | Behaviour | Why |
|---|---|---|
| iteration, `list()`, `len()`, `get()` | verified | route through `_fetch_all` |
| `count()`, `exists()`, `first()`, `last()` | **implemented correctly** | `count()`/`exists()` never reach `_fetch_all` (`query.get_count()`, `query.has_results()`); `first()`/`last()` are `[:1]`, so one colliding candidate returns `None` with a match in the next row. Affordable because §7.4 sizes truncation at `2 ≤ P·2^−b < √P` **by design** |
| slicing / pagination | **refused** | §7.5 states outright that pagination built directly on an indexed encrypted column is incorrect |
| `update()`, `delete()` | **refused** | would write to or destroy rows whose value differs — the only unrecoverable cases here |
| `aggregate()`, `values()`, `values_list()`, `only()`, `defer()` | **refused** | answered from SQL, or drop the column verification needs |
| `exclude()` | **refused** | see below |
| `Q` with `OR`/negation over an encrypted column | **refused** | a candidate may be present because another branch matched |

**`exclude()` is refused for a reason worth stating on its own:** the SQL excludes the whole bucket, so it drops rows it should have kept — and those rows never reach the adapter for §7.5 to put back. **A filter's false positives are recoverable; an exclusion's false negatives are not.**

`.candidates()` lifts every refusal. An escape hatch that refuses the same things is not one.

### The private-API cost is paid explicitly

`_fetch_all` is not a documented extension point, and this module *mirrors* its body rather than calling it, so candidates are dropped before `_prefetch_related_objects` runs. `tests/test_query_private_api.py` pins every assumption — that the method exists, that its body is still the two steps mirrored **and has not grown a third**, that `count()`/`exists()` still bypass the result cache, that `first()`/`last()` still slice, that chaining still funnels through `_clone` — each with a message saying what to re-verify. A Django upgrade now breaks the build instead of silently returning unverified rows.

---

## 2. Three defects found by writing the code

**`FIELDSEAL["CLIENT"]` was silently switching off E003.** `build_client` returns a supplied client without ever assembling the registry, so on that path the core never saw the model declarations and **neither the §7.4 band nor the §7.6 cardinality gate ran against them**. A project could declare a column at any truncation length, supply its own client, and get a clean `manage.py check`. The escape hatch E006 exists to police was disabling a different check entirely. Confirmed against the pre-fix code: `check_fieldseal` returned an empty list.

**`ValidationError` discards `code` and `params` when its message is a dict.** The machine-readable half has to be carried by the inner error; a caller who builds the dict themselves loses it with no warning. A test caught it.

**Where `on_unindexable="refuse"` raises is load-bearing.** The index can only be derived in `pre_save`, which runs *inside* the INSERT — so a `ValidationError` there propagates out of `Model.save()` and its `transaction.atomic(savepoint=False)` marks the connection for rollback. §10.1 asks for a form error; what that produces is a field error **and a transaction the caller cannot use**. The check now also lives in `Encrypted.validate()`, which `full_clean()` calls, so the `ModelForm` path fails before the database is touched. A direct `create()` still marks the transaction — Django's behaviour for any exception in `save()`, documented rather than pretended away.

---

## 3. `on_unindexable`, and §10.2's message

`bucket` needed **no query-path special-casing**, exactly as `docs/09` §7.2 predicted: a query derives the same marker unaided, and §7.5 separates two different unindexable values that share it — the case where re-verification does all the work rather than trimming a collision.

For §10.2's message (normative in shape), the core's own message correctly fails all three requirements — it addresses whoever wired the column. The adapter builds the user-facing half: names the character **and its position**, puts the fault on the system, offers a route ending with the value stored. **Locating the character uses the core as the oracle** rather than a second copy of the Unicode assignment table — that table decides index values, so a copy that drifts is a silent lookup miss. The engineer detail (`U+0378 at index 3`) goes to `params`, deliberately not into the sentence a person reads.

---

## 4. `warm()` — a drift, and a departure I made deliberately

**`docs/10` §4 has specified a sync `warm_blocking()` since the binding was written and the core did not have one** — the same shape of drift PR #61 found in the declaration-time gates. Added, and it **refuses inside a running event loop rather than deadlocking**: blocking on a coroutine from within the loop that would run it is a hang, and a hang at startup is diagnosed by guesswork.

**The `ready()` hook is opt-in, which departs from `docs/12` §7's wording.** `ready()` runs for `makemigrations`, `shell`, `collectstatic` and every test process — warming unconditionally makes a command that touches no encrypted row pay a KMS round trip and *fail when the key service is down*. **A migration blocked by a cold KMS is a worse failure than a cold cache.** §7 records the departure and the consequence it does not hide: under an `EnvelopeKeyProvider`, §8.2 confines unwrapping to `warm`, so something must prime the cache before the first read — the setting or `manage.py fieldseal_warm`, with no third option.

Warming covers **index keys as well as data keys** (spec §5.2 makes them siblings, so a cache warmed only for the DEK still stalls every indexed lookup — and the symptom reads as a slow query). Tenant-bound columns need their tenants named; a run that omits them **names what it skipped** rather than reporting a warm cache it did not warm.

`fieldseal_gen_uuids` prints and never edits. Its `--missing` mode reports only `table_uuid`: `column_uuid` is a required keyword argument, so a column without one does not construct — the first version looked for those too and would have reported nothing forever.

---

## 5. The cross-language test

**A row written b

author: alexliu190625
body:
Closes #1537.

DeepSeek-authored models routed through OpenRouter had reasoning turned off on
every request that did not explicitly ask for it, regardless of how the model
was configured. A model record that declares the `thinking_mode` ability still
got a disable payload on the wire, so the ability had no effect. The reason it
stayed off was that reasoning content produced on a tool-call chain has to be
replayed verbatim on the next request, and that replay did not exist yet. It
does now, so this change lets the declared ability decide.

## Behavior

Every row but the last describes a DeepSeek-authored model routed through
OpenRouter.

| Request | Model declares `thinking_mode` | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| No thinking configuration, non-streaming | no | disable payload sent | unchanged |
| No thinking configuration, non-streaming, no structured output | yes | disable payload sent | nothing sent; the endpoint's own default applies |
| No thinking configuration, streaming, no structured output | no | disable payload sent | unchanged |
| No thinking configuration, streaming, no structured output | yes | disable payload sent | nothing sent |
| No thinking configuration, any transport + `response_format` | either | disable payload sent | unchanged: still disabled, because provider reasoning can corrupt structured JSON whatever the transport |
| Thinking explicitly enabled or disabled by the caller | either | honored | unchanged |
| Model not authored by DeepSeek | either | no payload, apart from the structured-streaming rule above | unchanged |

A model that never declared the ability keeps its current request byte for
byte. Only records whose configuration asks for reasoning change.

Structured requests are the one shape where a declared ability does not open
the default. They keep the payload they had before this change on either
transport, so the JSON degrade-and-resend recovery in `chat` is not newly
relied on. Models from other authors keep the streaming-only form of that rule
they have always had.

## Deliberate divergence from the direct DeepSeek client

The direct DeepSeek client keeps disabling reasoning for every request that
does not ask for it, and does not consult abilities at all. That is intentional
and is stated in the code comment: it talks to a single endpoint whose default
it knows, while this client routes the same author's models through endpoints
whose defaults it does not control, and the declared ability is the only signal
available about what the operator wants. Aligning the two is a separate
decision about a different endpoint and is not made here.

## Capture-miss warning

The client already warns when a DeepSeek-served response comes back as a tool
call with no reasoning content under any recognized field name — the case where
the next request in the chain would fail with an unhelpful 400. That warning was
gated on "the caller asked for reasoning", which is exactly the condition this
change makes insufficient: the newly opened path never asks, the endpoint
reasons anyway, and the warning would never fire on the one path it now needs to
cover. The gate is now "this request did not go out with reasoning disabled",
computed from the same method that builds the request, so the warning and the
payload cannot disagree. Both hooks take the request's structured-output setting
for that reason: a structured request is disabled on either transport, so a
sentinel that assumed otherwise would report a miss against a response it had
itself made impossible. What each hook receives is the value the request it is
judging was built from, which on one degrade path differs from the value the
caller originally passed.

The rewritten gate agrees with the old one on every configuration that exists
before this change; what it adds is the one configuration this change creates.

Still not covered: an endpoint that ignores the disable payload, reasons anyway
and returns nothing under a recognized field name stays silent. That was true
before this change and is unchanged by it.

## Retry budget

One provider-compatibility retry rule replays the request with reasoning
disabled. For a model that declares the ability, that is now a real change to
the request rather than a no-op, so the rule fires where it used to be skipped
and spends one retry. Models that do not declare the ability are unaffected.
Covered by tests for both the non-streaming and the streaming path.

Against an endpoint that refuses every request not asking for reasoning
explicitly, recovery costs three upstream requests: the unspecified first
attempt, the disable attempt this rule now spends, and the enable attempt that
succeeds. The loop's four-request cap bounds it, and the test pins each
payload.

## Size and verification

| File | Added | Removed |
|---|---|---|
| `src/xagent/core/model/chat/basic/openrouter.py` | 115 | 50 |
| `src/xagent/core/model/chat/basic/openai.py` | 42 | 12 |
| `src/xagent/core/model/chat/basic/deepseek.py` | 2 | 1 |
| `tests/core/model/chat/basic/test_openrouter.py` | 736 | 40 |

- `pytest tests/core/model/chat/basic/` — 383 passed
- `pytest tests/core/model/chat/basic/test_openrouter.py` — 110 passed

Each added test was re-run against a build with the change deliberately undone,
to confirm it pins the new behavior rather than passing by accident:

- Dropping the ability check, so the default goes back to always-disabled: 12
  test cases fail, covering seven of the added tests once parameter
  combinations are counted.
- Narrowing the structured-output rule back to streaming only: four cases fail,
  all of them pinning the non-streaming structured shape.
- Widening that rule to models from other authors: the pre-existing test for a
  non-DeepSeek model asking for structured output fails, which is what keeps
  this change confined to DeepSeek-served models.
- Putting either capture-miss gate back on "the caller asked for reasoning":
  exactly one test fails, one per transport.
- Making either gate ignore the request's structured-output setting: exactly one
  test fails per transport, the ones pinning structured requests as disabled and
  silent.
- Handing the non-streaming gate the caller's original setting instead of the
  one its request was built from: the test covering the degrade-and-resend path
  fails on a warning about a capture that request had itself made impossible.

author: mattsavin
body:
Implements **P0-B** of docs/BUILD_IMPROVEMENTS.md. Independent of #32 (touches different server.ts regions; both may merge cleanly).

## Evidence recap
~1,900 5xx/week incl. 504s for GB users on `/api/auth/me` (127), `/` (126), `/api/gallery` (62) in the 2026-08-20..27 CF window. CF free-plan 504 = origin exceeded ~100s.

## Changes
1. `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` — was missing entirely; out-of-transaction writers hit the driver default (~1s) under lock contention.
2. `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` + boot-time `foreign_key_check` — schema declares REFERENCES but SQLite never enforced them. Risk note: enforcement on legacy data can turn latent violations into write failures; the boot check logs (read-only) any existing violations so we remediate with eyes open.
3. `slowRequestLog` middleware — outermost after trust proxy, `PERF_LOG=true` gates it, single-line `[PERF] {method,path,durationMs,status}` JSON for any request >1000ms, hooked on `close` so CF-abandoned hangs are captured. Permanent, negligible overhead.

## Repro attempt (spec task 4) — NOT reproduced locally
Prod-mode child server + **150 concurrent reads (100× /api/gallery, 50× /) while a raw writer held `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for 8s** on the same DB file:
```
requests: 150 | max latency: 76 ms | >5s: 0 | >1s: 0 | non-200: 0
```
**Read contention under WAL is not the mechanism.** The `/` static-path 504s can't be DB at all — that plus this result shifts suspicion to **event-loop starvation (sharp/bcrypt pools), host-level contention (prod + beta containers share the box), or the CF↔origin network path**. As spec'd, instrumentation ships anyway; we read a week of `[PERF]` docker logs before any code change beyond (1)(2)(3). Repro doubles as evidence the new pragmas are harmless under contention.

## Test plan
- [x] New unit tests: forces a >1s delay and asserts the exact `[PERF]` JSON shape; quiet for fast requests; fully inert without `PERF_LOG`
- [x] Full backend suite green (33 files / 327 tests), lint, prettier, typecheck, vite build
- [ ] CI green
- [ ] Post-merge: enable `PERF_LOG=true` in prod container env, read `docker logs` for `[PERF]` over the next week

## What changed

`pl.json` held **no `agents` namespace at all** — 0 of 563 keys — so the whole Builder rendered in English under `/pl`, the largest single gap in the catalog (#643). Translated all 563 keys as one namespace rather than piecemeal: a namespace is the unit a person reads, and seventy Polish strings among four hundred English ones reads worse than a consistently English panel.

Following the catalog's rules:
- **The product's own nouns stay English**, inflected into Polish grammar — agent, spec, capability, skill, embed, budget, run, prompt, provider, token, vault, workspace, sandbox, MCP — so a Polish reader meets the same words the docs, the API and the exported YAML use.
- **`secret` → `sekret`**, following the convention already in `pl.json` (22 uses, 0 English); `vault` stays English as it does there.
- **Counts are ICU `plural`** with Polish's `few`/`many` arms, never a ternary; a noun the number agrees with lives inside the plural.
- **Interpolations and `t.rich` tags preserved exactly.**

## How it was verified

- `messages/catalog.test.ts` green — agents complete, no half-sentences, no dead keys, no source duplication.
- `check:i18n` clean; prettier clean; `tsc` clean.
- Programmatic check: all 563 keys carry every `{interpolation}` their English source does, and every ICU block its Polish `few`/`many` forms; 0 empty values.

Closes #643

body:
## 为什么

统一 Agent 的 **B5 交互层**要落「Agent 主栏 + 对话词汇表」，但此前**没有任何设计依据**——设计系统主文档里零 agent 章节（grep 只命中付费确认弹窗和 logo）。

而 agent 状态在代码里是**四套互不认识的词表**：

| 在哪 | 现在的词表 |
|---|---|
| 消息 | `pending / streaming / done / error / cancelled` |
| 步骤徽标 | `done / active / warn` |
| 画布节点 | `idle / queued / running / success / error / recoverable` |
| 镜头占位卡 | 第四套（用 `phase` 不用 `status`） |
| **审批** | **没有词表**——靠 4 个独立 state 拼出来 |

后果：`AssistantTimeline` 吃 15 个 props，两个面板各 770 / 800 行，每加一种 agent 行为要同时改四处。没有依据就动手 = 再分裂一次。

## 改了什么

**新增 `docs/design/nomi-agent-interaction.md`**（主文档保持精简，只留指针）：

- **统一状态词表**：8 态 + 2 标志。`retryable` 挂在 `failed` 上、`deviated` 挂在 `done` 上，不再当独立态（现在的 `warn` 与 `done` 互斥是错的——事实是「做完了 **且** 和批准的不一样」）
- **对话词汇表 17 种**：承 master plan §4.3 的 12 种，补 5 种。其中两个是在**补真洞**：
  - `CanvasAssistantPanel.tsx:220` 在 `busy` 时静默丢弃用户输入（agent 忙时打字按回车，屏幕上什么都不发生）→ 指令队列
  - `agentUsageStore` 只有 runner 在写、**全仓零消费方**，等于白记 → 上下文用量
- **等待指示器改「工序图示」**：否决品牌 N（每条消息头已有 `NomiLogoMark`，一屏七八个；且 N=身份 ≠ 状态）。§6 因此划出「工序指示器」受管动效资产族，与通用图标（仍只许 tabler）分开
- **动效从 1 条 token 扩到 6 条** + 三条硬纪律：`prefers-reduced-motion` 全关 / 同屏最多 1 处扫光 / 暗色单独验
- **控件规格收口**：所有可点 = 28px、选择器药丸 vs 按钮 7px 方角、同排按钮等宽均分且主次只用颜色分、文字链不与按钮同排
- **参数条复用铁律**：计划卡/付费卡用**同一个** `InlineParameterBar`（控件由模型档案声明），批级 + 单镜覆盖两层。不在对话卡里另造参数 UI（那是并行版）

**解掉一处文档打架**（用户裁定）：付费确认在内嵌 agent 对话时长在**对话流内**，居中 `SpendConfirmDialog` 只留给画布直发与外部 MCP 驱动；两宿主共用同一个 `SpendConfirmRequest` 与同一份明细组件。

## 样张

`docs/design/mockups/2026-08-27-agent-conversation-vocabulary.html` — 浏览器直接打开，自动播放全流程 + **标尺开关**（蓝虚线=可点控件，应全部等高；黄虚线=文字链，唯一允许无高度的）。

真机跑过并逐项亲眼看过，据此修了一处代码里看不出的问题：摘要 pill 沿用节点上的 110px，在计划卡里会把「16:9 · 5s · 720p」截断成「…72…」，已改 150px 并把理由写进 §9。

## 关于 AI Elements

调研了 `vercel/ai-elements` 全部 48 个组件（HEAD `6a9d5b1` / 2026-08-21）。**一行代码都不搬**——它是 shadcn/ui + lucide + CVA 的另一套设计语言，装进来即撞 P1 且 `check:tokens` 当场红。只抄**状态机语义命名**与**组合式 slot 形态**，皮全部自绘（承 master plan §4.5）。

分诊：14 个是写代码 agent 专用（终端/测试/git/文件树…）与我们无关；7 个画布类我们自研的更强（它的 `canvas.tsx` 只有 26 行，就是包了层 ReactFlow）；11 个我们已有；真正可借鉴的是那 27 个对话类。

## 范围

**纯文档 + 样张，零代码改动。本文是实现依据，不是现状描述。** 已知缺口 7 条明列在 §12（浮层在滚动对话流里脱节、窄栏降级未定、暗色动效未验、英文片场话需二次创作…），不假装做完。

## 验证

`pnpm run gates` 八门全过（filesize / tokens / dangling-tokens / archetype-defaults / i18n / heavy-path / test-types / lint / typecheck / test / build）。

> ⚠️ 过程记录：首次跑 gates 时后台通知报「exit 0」，**哨兵文件是 `EXIT=1`**——真因是本 worktree 没装 `node_modules`，`tsx: command not found`。装完重跑才真绿。

body:
# Pull request

> Stacked on #94 → #93 → … → #85. The diff to review here is the last commit only.

## What and why

**Measured first, as the issue asks. The measurement said not to build the worker — and found a
severe freeze somewhere I would not have looked.**

| | Longest main-thread block, 200 devices |
|---|---|
| Before | **8,098 ms** |
| After | under 250 ms; worst single step **42 ms** |

No web worker. Two changes, neither of which is a thread.

### 1. A loop full of `await`s is still one task

Every `await` in the export settles on a **microtask** — `element.updateComplete` is one — and a
microtask continues the *same* task. So the loop painted nothing for its entire duration while
looking, in the source, like the most cooperative code imaginable.

`yieldToBrowser()` fixes it with a `MessageChannel` rather than `setTimeout(…, 0)`: after five
levels of nesting the specification clamps timers to 4 ms, and this yields once per device, so
500 devices would spend two seconds doing nothing but waiting for timers.

**8,098 ms → 5,609 ms.** Better. Still frozen.

### 2. ⚠️ I then measured the wrong thing and nearly shipped the fix for it

A comparison of `save()` against `save({ useObjectStreams: false })` reported **1158 ms against
6 ms**. That looks like an enormous free win, and I changed the code.

It was an artefact. Both were measured on the **same document**, and `pdf-lib` caches its
normalisation — so whichever call ran *second* was fast because the first had already done the
work. Measured properly on two separate documents, object streams are the **faster** of the two
(25 ms against 61 ms for sixty pages) *and* produce the smaller file. The change is reverted,
and the reasoning is in a comment where the next person will be standing.

### 3. The real cause: `embedPng` is lazy

It registers an embedder and does the decoding and deflating at **save** time. So two hundred
images were processed in one synchronous call *after the last progress callback*, while the loop
above behaved impeccably. Instrumenting by phase found it in a single run:

```
before=15  worstStep=15  after=5583   ← the block is after the loop
before=42  worstStep=42  after=24     ← after pdf.flush() inside the loop
```

`pdf.flush()` per device does that work where the yield can break it up.

Closes #36

## How it was tested

**`packages/web/test/pdf/responsiveness.browser.test.ts`** measures the **longest gap between
animation frames** — not total time, which a long export is allowed to have, but the longest
stretch in which nothing could be painted and no input handled. Kept as a test rather than run
once and written down, because "it was fine when I checked" is not a property anyone can rely on
six months later.

**It has a positive control, and this file needed it more than most.** A headless or
backgrounded browser throttles `requestAnimationFrame`, which would turn every number here into
a measurement of the harness. The control passing is what allowed the 5.6-second reading to be
believed rather than blamed on the runner (lesson L3).

**And a second assertion locates rather than detects**: the time between the last progress
callback and the finished document. A frame-gap number says "something blocked"; that one says
"the block is *after* the loop", which is the sentence that would have saved an hour.

Cancellation was already in from #91 and is now tested for the property that makes it true: the
export stops within a device or two of being told to. A cancel honoured after the remaining four
hundred devices have been drawn is not a cancel.

### On 200 rather than the issue's 500

500 devices is roughly a two-minute test, and the failure mode is not count-dependent — a block
at 200 exists at 500, proportionally larger. The per-device cost is now flat, so 500 devices is
2.5× the duration at the same responsiveness. Happy to raise it if you would rather have the
literal number in CI.

## Test-first confirmation

- [x] The test was written first and **observed failing** — at 8,098 ms against a 250 ms budget,
      which is about as unambiguous as a red test gets
- [x] The failure message described the missing behaviour

## Checklist

- [x] `npm run verify` is clean — 993 tests, 50 files
- [x] Coverage gates met
- [x] Every acceptance criterion in the issue is demonstrably met
- [x] User-visible strings wrapped in `msg()` — none added
- [x] No Matter payload or setup passcode is logged, or included in this PR's description
- [x] No ADR needed — and notably **no new dependency and no worker**, which is the outcome
      ADR 0013 hopes for

## Offline behaviour

Unchanged. Nothing here touches the network; this is entirely about how main-thread work is
distributed in time.

Completes the BFF side of **Item 1**. Follows #2406, #2414, #2420. Until now a refusal logged to console but a **successful issue wrote nothing** — so "which requester got a credential for which tool, when" was unanswerable after the fact. That's the one question an audit trail exists to answer. ## What it records Reuses the existing durable MCP audit store (LMDB, 5000-event cap) rather than adding another: ``` eventType: 'credential_issued' outcome: 'success' | 'refused' keyName, tool, aud, requester, jti, ttlMs ``` ## Metadata only — deliberately The credential value and the secret it was signed with are **absent from the record**. That store keeps 5000 events, so writing a 30-second secret into it would give the secret a long life — the opposite of the point. There's a test for exactly this, and **revert-to-RED confirms it**: adding `value` to the record fails that test, and only that test. ## Refusals go through one helper Three inline `throw`s became a single `refuse()` path, so no early return can silently skip the audit. A refused mint is precisely the event worth having a trail for — a revoked agent now leaves one instead of vanishing. ## Fire-and-forget The audit write is wrapped, matching `gatewayAudit`: an LMDB failure must not take out the request path it's observing. Covered by a test that makes the store throw and asserts issuance still succeeds. ## Verification | Suite | Result | |---|---| | Broker / endpoint / flag / audit | 21/21 | | Full BFF suite | 10,287 passed | The one failure was `src/__tests__/ciba.test.js`, which passes **61/61 in isolation**. The PR adds best-effort durable audit records for successful and refused JIT credential issuance while deliberately excluding credential material. - Records issuance metadata, expiration, and refusal reasons in the existing LMDB MCP audit store. - Consolidates broker-level refusals through a shared audited helper. - Adds tests for successful issuance, revocation refusal, secret exclusion, and audit-store failure tolerance.

The broker correctly audits its own explicit outcomes, but the endpoint rejects an unset key before entering the broker, making the newly added signing_secret_unset audit ineffective for the real request path. **Files Needing Attention:** demo_api_server/services/jitCredentialBroker.js, demo_api_server/routes/vaultServiceKey.js

author: zeidanreza
body:
Closes the **1.17 floor** from the beta plan — *"the false sentence must not survive to a beta
customer."* It was written to ride along with 1.3/1.13; those shipped in #194/#195 without it, and
no remaining planned PR opens `cfoReport.ts`, so it needed its own branch.

## The bug

`cfoReport.ts` printed this to every CFO who downloads the report, unconditionally:

> Cap monthly spend at $X (forecast plus a safety margin…). **The agent will pause and notify if it approaches this limit.**

There are **two mechanisms at two thresholds**, and that sentence was true of neither:

| | Fires at | Does | Conditional on |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Slack alert** | `alert_threshold_pct` — **80%** default | Posts to Slack, once per month | **Returns silently with no webhook** (`main.py:3460-3461`) |
| **Enforcement** | **100%** — at the cap | Rejects billable LLM calls with 429 (`_budget_gate`, `main.py:3569-3572`) | An `agent_budgets` row existing (`_budget_caps`, `:3592-3593`) |

So: "pause" is a 429 rejection, not a pause; "if it approaches" describes the *alert*, not
enforcement; and "notify" no-ops when no Slack webhook is configured. It was also promised to
readers who had set no budget at all.

## The fix

```diff
-… The agent will pause and notify if it approaches this limit.
+… Once set, Arceo stops the agent's paid model calls when it reaches the cap.
+  Connect Slack and it will warn you earlier — at 80% by default.
```

1.17's full fix was specified as *"condition on budget-set + capture-path."* **"Once set,"** carries
the budget-row requirement and **"Connect Slack"** carries the webhook requirement — so the whole
item lands in copy, with no new `CFOReportData` fields and no new API call.

The word *"Cap"* is kept because it's accurate: `saveBudget` writes the same `agent_budgets` row
that `_budget_caps` reads (`main.py:6225` → `:3558`), so the cap the PDF recommends is a real,
enforcing one.

Per the plain-English rule, "429" becomes *"stops the agent's paid model calls."*

**Not touched:** the CostPortfolio budget panel. It deliberately says *"spend alert"* and never
*"cap"*, and understates rather than overstates.

## Also

`CLAUDE.md:443` — the **last** `±15% after 7 days` string left anywhere in the repo, corrected to
the real gate (50 captured calls across 3+ distinct days in a rolling 7-day window). That line is
where the wrong number kept regenerating from; it's the same false claim that reached the Foundry
all-team call and the Sands Group review out loud.

## Verification

- **3 new regression tests**, and I confirmed they **fail against the old sentence** before keeping
  them — they assert no `/pause/i`, no `/approach/i`, no bare `/will notify/i`, and require
  `/once set/i` + `/connect slack/i`.
- `tsc --noEmit` clean · `vitest run` **12 passed** (was 9) · `vite build` clean · `eslint .` clean.

Same convention as the existing confidence-line pin: this PDF is the only artifact that reaches a
customer with no engineer attached, so its claims get regression coverage.

author: alexkorchagingit
body: ## Problem In production the app could sit forever on the splash screen or on «Загрузка турниров…». PostgREST calls through supabase-js did not always settle, so `isLoading` never flipped and the UI never left the spinner. Splash was extra-fragile: it required a loaded `account`. A failed/timed-out user lookup left `account = null` and kept the splash. Club cosmetics reset and the full user list also ran **before** the splash was allowed to dismiss. ## Fix - Every PostgREST `fetch` aborts at **5 seconds** (`AbortController` + `Promise.race` via `withTimeout`). - supabase-js retries are off. Requests use `credentials: 'omit'` and drop `X-Client-Info` so CORS preflight stays simple (`showdown-br.ru` → `api.showdown-br.ru`). - Boot: session lookup is capped at 5s. Cosmetics reset / club directory no longer block splash. If the account does not arrive, a watchdog logs the user out to the login screen (`user = null`, `isLoading = false`). - Tournaments: 5s timeout, `try/catch`, `setIsLoading(false)` always, `loadError` + **Повторить загрузку**. Tournament spinner is no longer tied to user loading. Also includes the earlier login OTP hang fix and email-before-consent flow (not yet on `main`). ## Verify 1. Chrome with a saved session: splash must end within ~5 seconds (home or login), never hang. 2. Tournaments tab: if the API is slow/down, after 5s show the error and retry — not «Загрузка турниров…» forever. 3. Retry reloads the list when the network is back.
